summary: Three women go to the tomb at sunrise with spices, worrying about who will move the stone, and find it already rolled back. Inside, a young man in white tells them Jesus has risen, shows them the empty place, and sends them to tell the disciples — and Peter by name — that he is going ahead to Galilee. They run out and say nothing to anyone, because they were afraid. That is where the oldest manuscripts stop. The verses that follow in most Bibles report appearances to Mary Magdalene, to two walkers, and to the eleven, a commission to preach everywhere, and the ascension.
whyItMatters: Mark's resurrection account is eight verses long, contains no appearance by Jesus, and ends on the word 'afraid.' Whether that was the intended ending is the single most consequential textual question in the New Testament, and you deserve to know about it before you read the chapter rather than after.

context.author: Anonymous; early tradition names Mark, recording Peter's preaching — note that the messenger names Peter specifically in verse 7
context.audience: Greek-speaking readers outside Judea, who would have known the risen Jesus story already from preaching before they ever read it here
context.date: Somewhere in the AD 50s–70s; verses 9-20 are generally dated later than the rest
context.setting: A rock-cut tomb outside Jerusalem, at sunrise on the first day of the week — the day after the Sabbath
context.literaryForm: Narrative, ending abruptly. The Greek of verse 8 finishes on a conjunction, which is an unusual way to end a sentence, let alone a book

keyVerses.text: He has risen! He is not here. See the place where they laid him!
keyVerses.why: The claim the whole faith rests on, delivered in a sentence, to three women, with an invitation to check the spot.

keyVerses.text: But go, tell his disciples and Peter, ‘He goes before you into Galilee. There you will see him, as he said to you.’
keyVerses.why: Peter is named separately — the man who denied him three times is singled out to be told.

keyVerses.text: They went out, and fled from the tomb, for trembling and astonishment had come on them. They said nothing to anyone; for they were afraid.
keyVerses.why: The last sentence in the oldest manuscripts. A book about people failing to understand ends with the news undelivered.

keyVerses.text: Go into all the world and preach the Good News to the whole creation.
keyVerses.why: From the longer ending — the commission that answers the silence of verse 8.

questions.question: Does Mark really end at verse 8? My Bible has twenty verses.
questions.answer: Both are true, and this is the honest situation. The two oldest complete Greek Bibles — Codex Sinaiticus and Codex Vaticanus, both fourth century — end Mark at verse 8. So do the oldest Syriac, an old Latin manuscript, and the earliest Armenian and Georgian versions. Eusebius and Jerome both wrote that the accurate copies known to them ended there. On the other side, verses 9-20 appear in the large majority of surviving Greek manuscripts and were quoted as scripture by the second century, so they are early. Nearly every modern Bible prints them with a note, a bracket, or a line break. The text hosted here prints them continuously.

questions.question: What is the actual evidence that 9-20 was added?
questions.answer: Four strands, and they are worth knowing rather than taking on trust. Manuscripts: the earliest and best copies lack it. Vocabulary and style: the Greek of these verses contains a notable cluster of words Mark never uses elsewhere, and the connective habits are different. Seams: verse 9 reintroduces Mary Magdalene as though she had not just been on stage in verses 1-8, which is what you would expect if the passage was written to be attached rather than composed in place. Variants: several different endings survive in the manuscript tradition — a shorter one, this longer one, both together, and this one with an extra insertion — which is the pattern you get when copyists are trying to solve a problem, not when they are transmitting an original.

questions.question: So did Mark intend to end at verse 8, or is the real ending lost?
questions.answer: Three positions, held by serious readers. First, it was lost — the last leaf of a scroll or codex is the most vulnerable part, and a book beginning as confidently as 1:1 seems unlikely to end mid-fear. Second, he intended it — the abruptness does what the whole book does, refusing to let the reader sit comfortably, and Mark has been telling you all along that people fail and are sent out anyway; verse 7 has already told you what happens next, so the reader knows what the women have not yet said. Third, he was prevented from finishing. There is no way to decide from the evidence available. What is not in dispute: verse 7 promises the disciples will see him in Galilee, so even the shortest version of Mark asserts the resurrection and points beyond itself.

questions.question: If those verses were added later, does that mean the resurrection is in doubt?
questions.answer: No, and it is worth being precise about why. The empty tomb and the announcement 'he has risen' are in verses 1-8, which nobody disputes. The appearances summarized in verses 9-20 are all independently recorded elsewhere — Mary Magdalene in John 20, the two walkers in Luke 24, the meal with the eleven in Luke 24 and John 20, the commission in Matthew 28, the ascension in Luke 24 and Acts 1. And Paul's list of resurrection witnesses in 1 Corinthians 15:3-8 is earlier than any of the gospels. The textual question is about how this particular book ends, not about whether the events were reported.

questions.question: Why do the women bring spices to a body that has been in a tomb since Friday?
questions.answer: Because the burial in 15:46 was done in a rush — Joseph took the body down as the Sabbath was starting and simply wrapped it in linen. The anointing that should have accompanied it never happened, and no work could be done on the Sabbath. So they come at the first possible moment, Sunday at sunrise. Mark also records them realizing on the way that they have no plan for the stone, which is the sort of practical detail that gives the scene its texture — they are expecting a corpse and a problem, not an announcement.

questions.question: Why does it matter that women found the tomb?
questions.answer: It matters as evidence, on a point historians of various convictions have noted. In first-century Jewish and Roman society, a woman's testimony carried little weight and was in some legal settings not accepted at all. If you were constructing a persuasive account, you would not make women the sole discoverers and first witnesses — you would use Peter, or a respected council member. All four gospels do it anyway, and Mark, the earliest, has no male witness at the tomb at all. It is the kind of detail that is difficult to explain except as something the tradition was stuck with.

questions.question: Who is the 'young man in a white robe'?
questions.answer: Mark describes him without naming him — a young man, seated on the right, in a white robe. Matthew calls the figure an angel, Luke has two men in dazzling clothes, John has two angels. Most readers take Mark's description as an angelic messenger; white is the standard marker for it. Some connect him to the young man who fled naked in 14:51-52, since Mark uses the same word, which would make a quiet arc from a man losing his clothes in panic to a man seated in white announcing the resurrection. It is a suggestion, not a proof.

questions.question: Why does the message single out Peter?
questions.answer: 'Tell his disciples and Peter' is three words that undo chapter 14. The last thing the reader saw Peter do was swear he never knew the man, and then weep. He is named separately here not to exclude him from the disciples but to make certain he knows he is included. If the old tradition is right that this gospel carries Peter's preaching, then the book that records his failure in the most damaging detail also preserves the sentence that came for him afterward.

questions.question: The women are told to speak and they say nothing. Is that a failure?
questions.answer: In the terms of the story, yes — the last human action in Mark's gospel is a command disobeyed out of fear. It fits everything before it: nobody in this book gets it right, from the Twelve to the crowds to the family. But the silence is clearly not permanent, since somebody eventually told this story or we would not have it. Mark leaves the gap open. Read one way it is bleak; read another it hands the reader the job the characters dropped.

questions.question: Verse 18 mentions picking up snakes and drinking poison. What is that about?
questions.answer: It sits in the longer ending, among signs said to accompany believers. Two of the five have clear parallels in Acts — Paul survives a snake bite in Acts 28:3-6, and healings run through the book. There is no instruction anywhere to attempt any of this deliberately. A small number of groups have read it as a command and handled venomous snakes in worship, with fatalities; the overwhelming majority of Christian traditions read it as a description of protection in the course of the mission, not a practice to seek out. Given the textual status of these verses, most readers are also cautious about building anything on them that is not supported elsewhere.

questions.question: How should I actually read this chapter, knowing all this?
questions.answer: A suggestion: read verses 1-8 and stop. Sit with an ending that gives you an empty tomb, an announcement, a promise that he has gone ahead, and three terrified women who say nothing — and notice that you, the reader, now know something nobody in the story has passed on. Then read 9-20 knowing what they are: an early and widely received summary of appearances recorded elsewhere, added by a hand other than the one that wrote the rest. Both readings are honest. Only pretending there is no question would not be.

glossary.term: The first day of the week
glossary.def: Sunday. The Sabbath ran Friday evening to Saturday evening, so this is the first moment work such as anointing a body could be done.
Two fourth-century Greek Bibles, the oldest surviving near-complete copies. Both end Mark at 16:8. Sinaiticus can be viewed online page by page.
Mark 16:9-20. Present in most manuscripts and quoted from the second century, absent from the earliest and best, and different in vocabulary and style from the rest of the book.
The discipline of comparing manuscript copies to work out what a text originally said. It is what produces the footnotes in modern Bibles, and this chapter is its most famous case.
To apply spices and oil to a body — here a burial rite that had been cut short by the Sabbath, which is why the women come at first light.
